claim: Gray, Lorie, Putzolu and Traiger 1976: lockable units form a tree (database, file, page, record) and a node is locked in S or X only after every ancestor is tagged with an intention mode (IS, IX, SIX); no measured gain, the paper gives no baseline, workload or scale.

Eswaran, Gray, Lorie and Traiger 1976: predicate locks guard against phantoms, but the general test of whether two predicates can be satisfied together is recursively unsolvable, so only a restricted simple class of predicates is usable; no measurement.

Lomet 1993: key-range locking locks the ranges between index keys with intention modes plus insert-into-range and delete-in-range modes, and merging range, key and record into one lock cuts the number of locks at a cost in concurrency; no measured figure, overhead is counted as the number of locks per operation.

Graefe 2010, a survey of B-tree locking (ACM TODS 35(3)): no measured gain; it cites Srinivasan and Carey 1991 as the one comparison of locking techniques (not opened) and states that fine locking is required most often at hot spots, such as the high end of a time-organized B-tree.

Ries and Stonebraker 1977, a simulation and not an engine: with 10 transactions over 5000 entities, each touching 50 to 500 entities, and lock I/O equal to entity I/O, useful I/O was 7041.957 with one granule, 9437.987 at 10 granules, 9572.718 at 20, 7359.828 at 500 and 3408.635 at 1000 granules (OCR text).

Ries and Stonebraker 1977 (same simulation): the best number of granules rises as transactions touch fewer entities, the parameter with the most effect being the number of entities touched, and in most cases 10 granules appears sufficient.

Microsoft Learn page 'Lock Escalation (Database Engine)', current version fetched 2026-11-19 with no version marker: a statement acquiring at least 5,000 locks on one table or index triggers escalation to a table lock, retried after each additional 1,250 locks; the instance-wide trigger is 24 percent of engine memory at about 100 bytes per lock; no measured gain given.

PostgreSQL documentation, chapter 13.3 Explicit Locking, current version fetched 2026-11-19: row-level locks are stored in the row, so there is no limit on the number of rows locked at one time and no escalation, at the cost that locking a row might cause a disk write; no measured gain given.

Graefe 2007 (BTW 2007, pp. 18-42): each lock structure takes 64-128 bytes in most implementations and acquiring and releasing one lock costs thousands of CPU cycles, so millions of locks need billions of cycles; these are stated figures with no experiment or benchmark behind them.

Graefe 2007: one ill-advised escalation to an index lock lets no other transaction update a B-tree entry, and with tens or hundreds of concurrent transactions the multi-programming level collapses; this is argument with no workload or count behind it, and the paper proposes de-escalation and intermediate granules.

Srinivasan and Carey 1993 (VLDB Journal 2(4), simulation of a centralised DBMS): with a 50/50 insert and delete mix, uniform keys, 40,000 entries in about 250 leaf pages, 200 entries per page, 1 CPU, 8 disks and multiprogramming level 0 to 100, record locks and leaf-page locks held to transaction end gave no difference at batching factor 1, but at batching factor 10 leaf-page locking performed much worse through deadlocks and re-executions; the size of that loss is in Figure 23 and was not read.

Srinivasan and Carey 1993 give the cause and the conclusion: about 40,000 record IDs against about 250 leaf pages gives very few deadlocks under record locking, and they conclude that a highly concurrent long-term lock holding strategy is needed, leaf-page locking being unlikely to suffice.

MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual, 17.7.1 InnoDB Locking (fetched 2026-11-19): gap locks do not conflict with each other and only block inserts, and insert-intention locks let inserts at different positions of one gap not wait for each other; no measured figure.

MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual, 17.7.1 InnoDB Locking: under REPEATABLE READ next-key locks are used for searches and index scans, which prevents phantom rows; setting READ COMMITTED disables gap locking except for foreign-key and duplicate-key checks, and the page calls gap locks part of the tradeoff between performance and concurrency.
